transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: A new study has found that children who spend more time playing outside have significantly better eyesight and lower rates of nearsightedness, or myopia, compared to children who spend most of their time indoors. The research, published in the *Journal of the American Medical Association*, followed over 4,000 children for five years and found that those who spent at least two hours a day outside were 50 percent less likely to develop myopia than children who spent less than 30 minutes a day outdoors. Scientists believe that natural light and looking at distant objects while outside help the eye develop properly and prevent it from growing too long, which is what causes nearsightedness. The study also found that the type of activity didn't matter as much as just being outside—whether kids were playing sports, just sitting in the sun, or reading outdoors, they all got similar benefits. Researchers say the findings are important because rates of myopia are rising rapidly around the world, especially in East Asian countries where children often spend long hours studying indoors. They recommend that parents and schools make sure children get plenty of time outside every day to protect their vision.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1. What did the new study find about outdoor time and children's eyesight?
2. Why is being outside good for eyesight according to scientists?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Female)
paras: The city of Edinburgh in Scotland has become the first city in the United Kingdom to introduce a tourist tax, charging visitors a small fee for each night they stay in hotels, hostels, and other accommodation. The tax, which is £2 per night per adult, will be used to fund public services, maintain tourist attractions, and keep the city clean and attractive for visitors. The city council says that Edinburgh welcomes over 4 million tourists every year, and while tourism brings significant economic benefits, it also puts pressure on public services, infrastructure, and local residents. The tourist tax is expected to raise about £15 million per year, which will be spent on things like street cleaning, maintaining public parks and historic sites, and supporting cultural events. The idea has been controversial—some hotel owners and tourism businesses are worried that the tax will discourage tourists from visiting and make Edinburgh more expensive than other cities. But supporters say the fee is small enough that most tourists won't mind, and that the benefits of better maintained attractions and cleaner streets will actually make the city more attractive to visitors. Several other cities in the UK are now considering introducing similar taxes.
Questions 3 to 5 are based on the news report you have just heard.
3. What new policy has Edinburgh introduced?
4. How much money is the tax expected to raise per year?
5. Why are some business owners worried about the tax?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: Engineers at the University of California have developed a new type of solar panel that can generate electricity from both sunlight and rainwater, making it possible to produce power even on cloudy, rainy days. Traditional solar panels only work when the sun is shining, which means they don't produce any electricity at night and produce less on cloudy or rainy days. The new panels have a special transparent coating on top that uses the kinetic energy of falling raindrops to generate small amounts of electricity through a process called triboelectric effect—essentially, the friction between the water droplets and the panel surface creates an electric charge. While the amount of electricity generated from rain is much less than what's generated from sunlight, it's enough to make solar power more reliable in places with lots of rain and cloudy weather. The researchers say the technology could be especially useful in tropical and subtropical regions that get a lot of rain, where traditional solar panels are less effective. The panels are still in the prototype stage, but the team is working on improving their efficiency and hopes to bring them to market within the next few years.
Questions 6 and 7 are based on the news report you have just heard.
6. What is special about the new solar panels?
7. Where could this technology be especially useful?

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (James): Hey Sophie, I heard you got a new cat! How's that going?
Woman (Sophie): Oh, it's amazing! Her name is Luna, and she's the sweetest thing. I adopted her from the shelter two weeks ago, and I already can't imagine life without her.
Man: That's awesome! I've been thinking about getting a pet too, but I can't decide between a cat and a dog. What made you choose a cat?

Woman: Well, I work full-time and I'm not home a lot during the day, so a dog wouldn't work for me. Dogs need a lot of attention and exercise—you have to walk them multiple times a day, and they get lonely if you're gone all the time. Cats are much more independent. They're fine being home alone during the day as long as they have food, water, and a litter box.
Man: Yeah, that's a good point. I work long hours too, so a dog might be difficult. But I've heard cats are aloof and don't really care about their owners. Is that true?

Woman: Oh, definitely not! Luna is so affectionate. She greets me at the door when I come home, she curls up on my lap while I watch TV, and she sleeps at the foot of my bed every night. She's not as demanding as a dog, but she still shows she loves you in her own way.
Man: That's nice. But what about the litter box? Isn't that gross to clean?

Woman: It's not my favorite thing, but it's really not that bad. You just have to scoop it every day and change the litter completely once a week. It takes like two minutes. And it's a lot easier than having to wake up early every morning to walk a dog in the rain and snow, right?
Man: That's true. What about scratching furniture? I've heard cats destroy couches and curtains.

Woman: They can if you don't give them something else to scratch. But if you get a good scratching post and train them to use it, they usually leave your furniture alone. Luna has a scratching post and she uses it all the time. She hasn't scratched anything she's not supposed to yet.
Man: Hmm, you're making a pretty good case for cats. What about costs? Is having a cat expensive?

Woman: It can be, but it doesn't have to be. The adoption fee was pretty cheap, and food and litter don't cost that much each month. The expensive part is vet bills—you have to make sure they get their shots and checkups, and if they get sick it can be really pricey. But that's true for any pet, right?
Man: Yeah, that makes sense. Do you think I should get a cat?

Woman: I think you'd love it! But you should think about it carefully. It's a big responsibility—cats can live 15 years or more, so it's a long-term commitment. You should also make sure your apartment allows pets.
Man: Oh right, I should check that first. My lease says something about pets, but I don't remember the exact rules.
Woman: Yeah, definitely check that before you do anything. And if you want, you can come over and meet Luna sometime. Spend some time with her and see how you like having a cat around.
Man: That would be great! Thanks, Sophie. I really appreciate all the advice.
Woman: No problem! Cats are the best, but they're not for everyone. It's better to think it through first than to get a cat and then realize you don't want one.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Maya): Hey David, what are you reading? You look really focused.
Man (David): Oh, hey Maya. I'm reading this book about the history of timekeeping—like how people have measured time throughout history. It's actually really fascinating.
Woman: The history of timekeeping? That sounds... kind of boring, honestly. Why are you reading about that?

Man: I thought it would be boring too, but it's actually really interesting. Did you know that before clocks were invented, people used to measure time using things like sundials, water clocks, and candle clocks? And the idea of dividing the day into 24 equal hours is actually pretty recent—for most of history, hours were different lengths depending on the season, because people divided daylight into 12 parts and nighttime into 12 parts.
Woman: Wait, really? So hours weren't always the same length? That's weird. How did people deal with that?

Man: Well, it worked for them because most people were farmers and their lives were tied to the sun anyway. It wasn't until trains and factories were invented that people needed more precise, standardized time. Before that, every town had its own local time based on when the sun was highest in the sky. But when trains started running between cities, they needed a consistent schedule, so they had to standardize time zones.
Woman: That's wild. I never thought about why we have time zones. So when did clocks get invented?

Man: The first mechanical clocks were invented in Europe in the 13th and 14th centuries, but they were really inaccurate—they could lose or gain hours in a day. They were mostly used in churches and monasteries to call people to prayer. It wasn't until the 17th century, when the pendulum clock was invented, that clocks became accurate enough to measure minutes and seconds.
Woman: Wow, that's later than I thought. And now we have all these super accurate atomic clocks that are perfect, right?

Man: Yeah, atomic clocks are incredibly accurate—they lose less than a second over millions of years. But the funny thing is, even though we can measure time more precisely than ever, we still don't really understand what time actually is. Physicists still argue about it.
Woman: That's mind-blowing. We use time every single day, but we don't even know what it is.

Man: I know, right? That's what makes it so interesting. The book talks about all that—how our perception of time changes depending on what we're doing, how time seems to fly when you're having fun and drag when you're bored. There's all this psychology and philosophy around time too, not just physics.
Woman: Hmm, you've convinced me. That actually does sound interesting. Can I borrow that book when you're done with it?
Man: Sure! I'm almost finished with it. I'll give it to you next week.
Woman: Great, thanks! I never thought I'd be interested in the history of time, but you make it sound really cool.
Man: That's what I love about reading—you discover all these fascinating things you never would have thought to learn about otherwise.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: The history of coffee is a story that spans over a thousand years and crosses continents, from the ancient highlands of Ethiopia to coffee shops around the world today. Coffee is now one of the most popular beverages in the world, with over 2 billion cups consumed every day, but its origins are shrouded in legend.

According to one famous legend, coffee was discovered by an Ethiopian goat herder named Kaldi who noticed that his goats became unusually energetic and couldn't sleep at night after eating the red berries from a certain bush. Curious, he tried the berries himself and experienced the same stimulating effect. He shared his discovery with local monks, who began using the berries to stay awake during long hours of prayer.

Whether this legend is true or not, we do know that coffee was first cultivated and consumed in the Arabian Peninsula, in what is now Yemen, by the 15th century. From there, it spread to other parts of the Middle East and North Africa, and coffee houses—called qahveh khaneh—became important social and intellectual centers where people gathered to drink coffee, talk, play games, and listen to music.

Coffee came to Europe in the 17th century, brought by traders and travelers from the Middle East. At first, it was controversial—some people called it the "bitter invention of Satan" and tried to ban it. But it quickly became popular, and coffee houses opened in cities across Europe, becoming places where people gathered to discuss ideas, do business, and share news. In London, coffee houses were called "penny universities" because you could buy a cup of coffee for a penny and listen to and participate in intellectual discussions.

The Dutch were the first to bring coffee plants out of the Middle East and start growing them in their colonies in Indonesia and South America, breaking the Arab monopoly on coffee production. By the 18th century, coffee was being grown in the Caribbean, Central America, and South America, and Brazil had become the world's largest coffee producer—a title it still holds today.

Today, coffee is a global industry worth hundreds of billions of dollars, and it plays an important role in the economies of many developing countries. From its humble origins as a wild berry in Ethiopia to the lattes and cappuccinos we drink today, coffee has come a long way, and it continues to be an important part of social life and culture around the world.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: Color psychology is the study of how colors affect our emotions, behavior, and perceptions. While some ideas about color psychology are more myth than science, research has shown that colors can indeed have measurable effects on how we feel, think, and behave.

One of the most well-documented effects is the impact of color on mood. Warm colors like red, orange, and yellow are generally associated with energy, warmth, and excitement, but they can also evoke feelings of anger or danger. Red, in particular, has been found to increase heart rate and adrenaline levels, which is why it's often used for stop signs, fire alarms, and sale signs—it grabs our attention and makes us react quickly.

Cool colors like blue, green, and purple, on the other hand, are generally calming and relaxing. Blue, in particular, has been found to reduce stress and lower blood pressure, which is why it's often used in hospitals, offices, and bedrooms. Green is associated with nature and health, and it's often used in environmental branding and healthcare settings.

Colors can also affect our performance and behavior. For example, studies have found that the color red can negatively affect performance on academic tests, possibly because it's associated with danger and failure, which creates anxiety. On the other hand, blue has been found to enhance creativity and problem-solving, possibly because it's associated with calm and openness.

In marketing and advertising, color psychology is used extensively to influence how consumers perceive brands and products. Fast food chains often use red and yellow in their logos and decor because these colors stimulate appetite and create a sense of urgency and excitement. Luxury brands often use black, gold, and purple to convey elegance, sophistication, and exclusivity. Eco-friendly brands often use green to signal their commitment to the environment.

However, it's important to note that the effects of color are not universal—they can be influenced by culture, personal experience, and context. For example, while white is associated with purity and weddings in Western cultures, it's associated with mourning and funerals in many East Asian cultures. And our personal associations with colors—like if your favorite childhood toy was blue, or if you had a bad experience in a red room—can also affect how we respond to different colors.

Despite these limitations, color psychology remains a fascinating field that shows how much our environment, even something as simple as the colors around us, can shape our thoughts, feelings, and behavior in ways we might not even notice.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: Urban agriculture—the practice of growing food and raising animals in cities—has been growing in popularity around the world in recent years, as people look for ways to eat healthier, reduce their environmental impact, and build stronger communities. From small backyard gardens to large community farms to rooftop gardens on top of skyscrapers, urban agriculture takes many forms and offers many benefits.

One of the most obvious benefits of urban agriculture is that it provides fresh, healthy, locally grown food to city residents. In many low-income neighborhoods, often called "food deserts," there are no full-service grocery stores, and people have to rely on convenience stores and fast food restaurants that mostly sell unhealthy, processed food. Community gardens and urban farms can help address this problem by providing fresh fruits and vegetables at affordable prices, or even for free.

Urban agriculture also has environmental benefits. Growing food locally reduces the need for long-distance transportation, which saves fuel and reduces greenhouse gas emissions. Urban gardens can also help reduce the "heat island" effect in cities, where concrete and asphalt absorb heat and make cities hotter than surrounding rural areas. Plants and trees provide shade and cool the air through evaporation. Gardens also help manage stormwater by absorbing rainwater, reducing flooding and pollution from runoff.

Social benefits are another important aspect of urban agriculture. Community gardens bring people from different backgrounds together, creating opportunities for neighbors to meet, work together, and build relationships. They provide educational opportunities for children and adults to learn about food production, nutrition, and environmental science. And for many people, gardening is a relaxing, therapeutic activity that reduces stress and improves mental health.

Urban agriculture also has economic benefits. It can create jobs in farming, distribution, and food processing. It can also increase property values in neighborhoods with community gardens. And for people who grow their own food, it can save money on groceries.

Of course, urban agriculture also faces challenges. Space is limited in cities, and finding land for gardens can be difficult. Soil in urban areas is often contaminated with lead and other pollutants, so it has to be tested and sometimes replaced with clean soil. Water access can also be a problem. And climate change brings challenges like heat waves, droughts, and heavy rains that can damage crops.

Despite these challenges, urban agriculture continues to grow and evolve. New technologies like hydroponics, vertical farming, and rooftop greenhouses are making it possible to grow more food in less space. And as more people recognize the benefits of growing food locally, urban agriculture is likely to become an increasingly important part of how we feed our cities in the future.
